claims.text: A high density of grain boundaries in nanocrystalline high-entropy transition-metal catalysts balances surface vacancy and self-interstitial mobilities.
Local lattice distortions are responsible for the proposed balance between vacancy and interstitial mobilities.
Balanced defect mobilities promote self-healing of poisoned active sites and thereby improve catalytic durability.
The W-Ta-V-Cr high-entropy alloy is a single-phase BCC tungsten-based alloy with a bimodal grain-size distribution dominated by grains no larger than 100 nm.
The W-Ta-V-Cr alloy has been shown to achieve defect recombination under harsh environments.
Controlled annealing can create same-composition W-Ta-V-Cr catalysts with different grain sizes and grain-boundary densities while preserving phase composition.
Approximately 1073 K is a harsh operating temperature at which defect dynamics can significantly influence catalytic performance.
The cited W-Ta-V-Cr alloy has been tested at 1073 K under energetic-particle irradiation.
The cited evidence establishes behavior of the alloy under oxidizing or reactive catalytic atmospheres.
Local lattice distortions in high-entropy alloys produce a rugged energy landscape that makes vacancy and interstitial mobilities similar.
Grain boundaries act as effective sinks for vacancies and interstitials and promote their recombination.
Defect recombination prevents accumulation of deactivating surface defects or catalytic poisons.
Preventing defect or poison accumulation maintains active-site integrity and catalytic activity over time.
Nanocrystalline catalysts with high grain-boundary densities will retain turnover frequency longer and deactivate more slowly than coarse-grained counterparts.
Coarse-grained high-entropy catalysts have imbalanced defect mobilities that cause defect accumulation and faster catalytic degradation.
The proposed mechanism should apply to high-entropy transition-metal catalysts at elevated temperatures where defects are mobile.
The proposed mechanism may not apply at low temperatures or to conventional catalysts with low lattice distortion.
Failure of the high-grain-boundary catalyst to deactivate more slowly than the coarse-grained control would falsify the proposed durability advantage.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis attributes equalized defect mobilities to lattice distortions inherent to the high-entropy alloy, yet the chemically and phase-identical coarse-grained baseline is said to have imbalanced mobilities. Grain coarsening changes boundary density but does not, as described, remove the alloy's inherent lattice distortion.
